correct_citation: Hernandez, D. J. (2011). Double Jeopardy: How Third-Grade Reading Skills and Poverty Influence High School Graduation. Annie E. Casey Foundation. ERIC ED518818.
design: descriptive (graduation rates by reading group and poverty; no regression adjustment)
population_location: U.S. national, NLSY79 children born 1979-1989, n=3,975
outcome: Not graduating from high school by age 19
effect_as_reported: Not graduating by 19: 4% proficient vs 16% not proficient (four times); 9% basic; 23% below basic
excerpt: The rates are highest for the low, below-basic readers: 23 percent of these children drop out or fail to finish high school on time, compared to 9 percent of children with basic reading skills and 4 percent of proficient readers.
note: Full text. 3,975, PIAT Reading Recognition, NLSY79, age 19 all stated. Reading groups are top/middle/bottom thirds of PIAT scores, mapped roughly to NAEP levels; third-grade score is imputed from grades 2/4 when missing. Descriptive rates only; no adjustment for prior achievement or attendance.

correct_citation: Lesnick, J., Goerge, R. M., Smithgall, C., & Gwynne, J. (2010). Reading on Grade Level in Third Grade: How Is It Related to High School Performance and College Enrollment? Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago.
design: longitudinal cohort; correlation plus multilevel regression (students in schools) controlling for demographics and third-grade school effects
population_location: Chicago Public Schools, focus cohort of about 26,000 third graders (ITBS)
outcome: Eighth-grade ITBS reading
effect_as_reported: r=0.67 between grade 3 and grade 8 ITBS reading; about 40% of below-level third graders also below level in grade 8; group differences remain after covariates
excerpt: about 40 percent were also below grade level in eighth grade. Multilevel regression models that take into account third-grade school effects and demographic characteristics of students affirm the importance of third-grade reading level.
note: Full text. r=0.67 and 26,000 cohort stated in the executive summary. Third grade is the baseline, so there is no earlier-achievement control; attendance not a control.

correct_citation: Lesnick, J., Goerge, R. M., Smithgall, C., & Gwynne, J. (2010). Reading on Grade Level in Third Grade: How Is It Related to High School Performance and College Enrollment? Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago.
design: longitudinal cohort; multilevel regression adding grade 8 reading, grade 9 school and grade 9 course performance
population_location: Chicago Public Schools cohort of about 26,000 third graders followed to graduation and college
outcome: Five-year high school graduation; college enrollment
effect_as_reported: Graduated in 5 years: nearly 80% above level, 60% at level, 45% below level; with ninth-grade performance in the model, third-grade level no longer predicts graduation; only above-level predicts college attendance among graduates
excerpt: When ninth-grade performance was included as a predictor, being below- or at-grade-level was no longer a significant predictor of high school graduation or college attendance.
note: Full text. 80/60/45 rates stated in the executive summary (the report says 'in 5 years'). Executive summary: above grade level kept a significant relationship only for college attendance among graduates. Later models adjust for grade 8 achievement and grade 9 course performance (which includes absences).

correct_citation: Harding, J. F., Herrmann, M., Hanno, E. S., & Ross, C. (2019). Using kindergarten entry assessments to measure whether Philadelphia's students are on-track for reading proficiently. REL Mid-Atlantic / IES. ERIC ED599402.
design: predictive validity study; correlations and a threshold classification index
population_location: School District of Philadelphia kindergarten cohort 2014/15 (KEI) to grade 3 PSSA ELA 2017/18
outcome: Grade 3 PSSA ELA score and proficiency
effect_as_reported: r=0.42 (Emerging Academic Competencies) and 0.32 (Learning Engagement); threshold of 6 correctly predicted 53% of proficient and 73% of non-proficient students
excerpt: Emerging Academic Competencies had a correlation of 0.42 with ELA scores on the grade 3 PSSA, and Learning Engagement Competencies had a correlation of 0.32 with the same grade 3 test scores
note: Full text. 53%/73% stated in the summary and results; those figures come from the cohort not used to set the threshold. Unadjusted correlations; no control for other prior achievement or attendance.

correct_citation: Harding, J. F., Herrmann, M., Hanno, E. S., & Ross, C. (2019). Using kindergarten entry assessments to measure whether Philadelphia's students are on-track for reading proficiently. REL Mid-Atlantic / IES. ERIC ED599402.
design: descriptive correlations (unweighted pairwise)
population_location: School District of Philadelphia 2014/15 kindergarten cohort, random sample used to set the threshold
outcome: Grade 3 PSSA ELA score
effect_as_reported: Spring AIMSweb correlation with grade 3 PSSA ELA: K 0.50, G1 0.53, G2 0.73, G3 0.72
excerpt: The strength of the associations between AIMSweb scores and grade 3 PSSA scores generally increased from kindergarten to grade 3 (0.50 to 0.73; table 6).
note: Full text, Table 6. All four values match. The source says 'generally increased', because grade 3 (0.72) is slightly below grade 2 (0.73). Unadjusted.

correct_citation: Schlesinger, M., Saleet, G., Stewart, K., & Mosher, K. (2021). Four-year analysis of 2015-16 Kindergarteners' aimswebPlus reading and PSSA performance from 2015-16 to 2018-19. School District of Philadelphia, Office of Research and Evaluation.
design: descriptive cohort analysis (average national percentile ranks; no covariates)
population_location: Philadelphia 2015-16 kindergarten cohort with complete aimswebPlus and grade 3 ELA PSSA data, n=4,194
outcome: aimswebPlus performance group; grade 3 ELA PSSA level
effect_as_reported: Fall-K average NPR by later PSSA level: Advanced 72, Proficient 55, Basic 41, Below Basic 29
excerpt: The average student generally fell in the same aimswebPlus performance group in spring of third grade (2018-19) as where they started in fall of kindergarten (2015-16).
note: Full text. NPRs 72/55/41/29 appear in Figure 9 and Table A6. Table A6's n column appears reversed (Advanced listed as 1075) relative to Table 4 (Below Basic 1075, Advanced 264), but the NPR values are consistent with the figure. The sample is a quarter of the cohort with complete testing. No adjustment.

correct_citation: Jordan, E., McKenzie, S. C., & Ritter, G. W. (2018). Long-Term Outcomes of Low-Achieving Third Grade Readers. Arkansas Education Report, 16(3). Office for Education Policy, University of Arkansas.
design: descriptive longitudinal cohort analysis
population_location: Arkansas public school students, three cohorts entering grade 3 in 2008-09 to 2010-11
outcome: Reaching state-average reading by high school (average z-score of 0 over grades 8-10)
effect_as_reported: 11.5% of low-achieving third-grade readers caught up (14%, 11%, 10% by cohort); white, female and economically advantaged students more likely to catch up
excerpt: Overall, 11.5% of students who demonstrated low reading ability in third grade had “caught up” to average reading performance by high school.
note: Full text. Low-achieving means half an SD or more below the mean, about the lowest 20-25%. Detail: for Cohort 3 catching up was averaged over grades 8 and 9 only, because grade 10 scores were not available. Descriptive; no adjustment.

correct_citation: Duncan, G. J., Dowsett, C. J., Claessens, A., Magnuson, K., Huston, A. C., Klebanov, P., Pagani, L. S., Feinstein, L., Engel, M., Brooks-Gunn, J., Sexton, H., Duckworth, K., & Japel, C. (2007). School Readiness and Later Achievement. Developmental Psychology, 43(6), 1428-1446. ERIC EJ779938.
design: regression on six longitudinal data sets plus a meta-analysis of the coefficients
population_location: Six longitudinal data sets (countries not named in the abstract)
outcome: Later school reading and math achievement
effect_as_reported: Strongest predictors: school-entry math, reading and attention; meta-analysis ranks math > reading > attention; socioemotional behaviors generally insignificant
excerpt: A meta-analysis of the results shows that early math skills have the greatest predictive power, followed by reading and then attention skills.
note: Abstract only (ERIC record). Abstract says most models control for pre-school-entry cognitive, attention and socioemotional skills and family background, which matches the claim. Authors and journal details match ERIC.

correct_citation: Herbers, J. E., Cutuli, J. J., Supkoff, L. M., Heistad, D., Chan, C.-K., Hinz, E., & Masten, A. S. (2012). Early Reading Skills and Academic Achievement Trajectories of Students Facing Poverty, Homelessness, and High Residential Mobility. Educational Researcher, 41(9), 366-374. ERIC EJ987215.
design: longitudinal growth modeling
population_location: 18,011 students grouped by socioeconomic risk (location not stated in the abstract)
outcome: Growth in reading and math achievement, grades 3-8
effect_as_reported: First-grade oral reading and risk status predicted growth; risk predicted beyond early reading and moderated the early-reading link
excerpt: Socioeconomic risk and oral reading ability in first grade predicted growth of reading and math achievement in Grades 3 through 8.
note: Abstract only. All claim elements are in the abstract. The abstract does not describe covariates beyond risk status and early reading.

correct_citation: Juel, C. (1988). Learning to Read and Write: A Longitudinal Study of 54 Children from First through Fourth Grades. Journal of Educational Psychology, 80(4), 437-447. ERIC EJ389953.
design: small longitudinal study
population_location: 54 children, grades 1-4 (location not stated in the abstract)
outcome: Reading and writing ability at grade 4
effect_as_reported: Poor grade 1 readers almost invariably poor readers at end of grade 4; early reading predicted later ability better than early writing
excerpt: Poor first-grade readers almost invariably were poor readers at completion of grade four. Poor readers tended to become poor writers. Early writing skill did not predict later ability as well as did early reading ability.
note: Abstract only (short ERIC abstract). No adjustment described.

correct_citation: Lacoe, J., & Steinberg, M. P. (2019). Do Suspensions Affect Student Outcomes? Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 41(1), 34-62. ERIC EJ1204837.
design: student fixed effects and instrumental variables (district-wide policy change)
population_location: School District of Philadelphia student panel data
outcome: Math and reading achievement; peer achievement and absences
effect_as_reported: Suspension decreases suspended students' math and reading achievement; very small negative peer achievement spillovers from serious-misconduct suspensions; no change in peer absences
excerpt: A suspension decreases math and reading achievement for suspended students. The effects are robust to IV estimates leveraging a district-wide policy change in suspension use.
note: Abstract only. Student fixed effects absorb stable student differences, including baseline achievement. Effect sizes are not given in the abstract.

correct_citation: Steinberg, M. P., & Lacoe, J. (2017). The Academic and Behavioral Consequences of Discipline Policy Reform: Evidence from Philadelphia. Thomas B. Fordham Institute. ERIC ED598616.
design: difference-in-differences (district vs other PA districts for suspensions; student and school-compliance groups for outcomes, labelled 'associational' by the authors)
population_location: School District of Philadelphia, 2012-13 code-of-conduct reform
outcome: Suspensions, absences, math and ELA achievement
effect_as_reported: Previously conduct-suspended students: 1.45 fewer absences, no change in achievement; no long-term impact on conduct suspensions; peers in partial- and non-complier schools -0.06 SD math (non-compliers also -0.03 SD ELA); full compliers no significant change
excerpt: Students suspended prior to the policy change had 1.45 fewer school absences in the year after the change, compared to students who were not suspended pre-reform (see Figure 6, Panel B).
note: Full text. Numbers and direction all hold. Mismatch: the comparison group for the 1.45 figure is students without a conduct suspension in the pre-reform year (2011-12), not 'never-suspended' students. 'Never-suspended' describes the peer analysis. Authors call the student-level estimates associational. The models use student fixed effects and control for observables, but not for time-varying factors.

correct_citation: Lacoe, J., & Steinberg, M. P. (2018). Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes. Peabody Journal of Education, 93(2), 207-227. ERIC EJ1179434.
design: difference-in-differences (district level)
population_location: School District of Philadelphia, 2012-13 discipline reform
outcome: Suspensions, serious incidents, truancy, district math and ELA achievement
effect_as_reported: Modest decline in nonviolent-infraction suspensions in reform year; total suspensions unchanged; serious incidents up; truancy up; district math and ELA achievement down
excerpt: Philadelphia's reform resulted in a modest decline in suspensions for nonviolent infractions in the year of reform; however, total suspensions remained unchanged while serious incidents of student misconduct increased.
note: Abstract only. The truancy and achievement declines are in the next abstract sentence. The claim's closing 'mixed result' phrase is an interpretation, not a quoted finding. No effect sizes in the abstract.

correct_citation: Balfanz, R., Byrnes, V., & Fox, J. (2014). Sent Home and Put Off-Track: The Antecedents, Disproportionalities, and Consequences of Being Suspended in the Ninth Grade. Journal of Applied Research on Children, 5(2), Article 13. ERIC EJ1188519.
design: longitudinal cohort; descriptive rates plus logistic regression controlling for demographics, attendance and course performance
population_location: Florida statewide, 181,897 first-time ninth graders in 2000-01
outcome: High school graduation; dropout; postsecondary enrollment
effect_as_reported: First suspension: graduation chance drops from 3 in 4 to about half, dropout chance doubles; each additional suspension lowers graduation odds by 20% and postsecondary enrollment odds by 12%
excerpt: each additional suspension further decreases a student’s odds of graduating high school by 20%, and decreases their odds of enrolling in post-secondary schooling by 12%.
note: Full text. Suspensions are out-of-school suspensions. The regression controls for attendance and course performance but not for prior test achievement. The authors use 'impact' language; the design is correlational, as the claim says.

correct_citation: Bacher-Hicks, A., Billings, S. B., & Deming, D. J. (2019). The School to Prison Pipeline: Long-Run Impacts of School Suspensions on Adult Crime. NBER Working Paper No. 26257.
design: quasi-experimental: school-boundary change (plus principal-switch design), conditioning on baseline test scores
population_location: Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, middle school students around the 2002 boundary change
outcome: Dropout, four-year college attendance, adult arrest and incarceration, achievement
effect_as_reported: 1 SD stricter middle school: +1.7 pp dropout (15%), -2.4 pp four-year college (11%), 15-20% more likely arrested and incarcerated; no significant achievement impact
excerpt: schools that are one standard deviation stricter are 1.7 percentage points more likely to drop out of school (a 15 percent increase) and 2.4 percentage points less likely to attend a 4-year college (an 11 percent decrease).
note: Full text (working paper, not peer reviewed). The 15-20% arrest and incarceration figure is in the abstract. The text says 'no statistically significant impact on achievement'. Models condition on a cubic of prior-year test scores.

correct_citation: Sorensen, L. C., Bushway, S. D., & Gifford, E. J. (2021). Getting Tough? The Effects of Discretionary Principal Discipline on Student Outcomes. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-216, Annenberg Institute at Brown University (Education Finance and Policy, 2022, 17(2), 255-284).
design: variation in principal propensity to remove (PTR) students; linked administrative records with fixed effects
population_location: North Carolina middle schools, 2008-2016 linked discipline, education and justice records
outcome: Minor misconduct, high school graduation, absences, test scores

excerpt: to the 90th percentile of PTR would thereby increase absences by 0.5 days, reduce test scores by 0.02 standard deviations, increase grade retention rates by 0.4 percentage points, and decrease graduation rates by 2.7 percentage points.
note: Full text, February 2021 version. Journal details (EFP 17(2) 255-284, 2022) were confirmed via Crossref metadata (DOI 10.1162/edfp_a_00341); the journal text was not fetched.

correct_citation: Chu, E. M., & Ready, D. D. (2018). Exclusion and Urban Public High Schools: Short- and Long-Term Consequences of School Suspensions. American Journal of Education, 124(4), 479-509. ERIC EJ1186270.

population_location: New York City public high school students

correct_citation: Anderson, K. P., Ritter, G. W., & Zamarro, G. (2019). Understanding a Vicious Cycle: The Relationship between Student Discipline and Student Academic Outcomes. Educational Researcher, 48(5), 251-262. ERIC EJ1220624.

outcome: Test scores and grade retention
effect_as_reported: Exclusionary consequences related to worse test scores and more retention than less exclusionary ones; may be driven by selection bias
excerpt: However, despite controlling for a robust set of covariates, sensitivity checks demonstrate that the estimated relationships between consequences and academic outcomes may still be driven by selection bias into consequence type.
note: Abstract only. The abstract does not say whether prior achievement is among the covariates.

correct_citation: Hwang, N. (2018). Suspensions and Achievement: Varying Links by Type, Frequency, and Subgroup. Educational Researcher, 47(6), 363-374. ERIC EJ1189786.

correct_citation: Noltemeyer, A. L., Ward, R. M., & Mcloughlin, C. (2015). Relationship between School Suspension and Student Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. School Psychology Review, 44(2), 224-240. ERIC EJ1141532.

note: Abstract only. Everything except the last clause is in the abstract. The abstract does not say the pooled studies are mostly correlational, so that detail is not shown. Pooled effect sizes are not given in the abstract.
